extracted.intended_audience: zoologists, naturalists, and biology students studying Hydra and freshwater coelenterates (taxonomists and field biologists)
extracted.subtask_description: Diagnostic and natural-history criteria for identifying, describing, and studying Hydra and related freshwater/brackish coelenterates, including morphology, life-cycle, behavior, and habitat notes. Suitable for taxonomic identification and biological observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial fission cell-layer requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a piece to be formed by artificial fission it is necessary for the piece to contain cells of both cell-layers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies that regenerative success after artificial fission depends on including both ectoderm and endoderm in the fragment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg development sequence (Hydra)
rubrics_metrics.description: Egg is fertilized at the base of the ectoderm; upon emergence it splits to form a hollow mass of comparatively large equal cells; smaller cells separate and fill the central cavity; a delicate mucus film is secreted over the egg; larger cells secrete a thick chitinous (horny) egg-shell and within it a delicate membrane; repeated cell division produces an oval hollow embryo which escapes into the water by disintegration of the egg-shell and rupture of the inner membrane; tentacles and mouth form and the column attaches by the aboral pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this sequence to recognize developmental stages: segmentation → mucus covering → chitinous shell formation → formation of hollow embryo → escape by shell disintegration → formation of tentacles and mouth → attachment by aboral pole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egg morphology and shell ornamentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indian eggs are spherical; the shell bears relatively long spines expanded, flattened and more or less divided at the tip; the part of the egg in contact with the parent-polyp is bare. Eggs are sometimes produced without shells (probably unfertilized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Egg-shell ornament (spines: long, flattened, divided at tip) is a diagnostic character; absence of shell may indicate unfertilized eggs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic key distinguishing Hydra species
rubrics_metrics.description: Key: I. Colour leaf-green; cells contain green (chlorophyll) corpuscles → viridis. II. Colour never leaf-green; no chlorophyll corpuscles. A. Tentacles comparatively stout, habitually shorter than the column; column cylindrical when gastral cavity empty; largest nettle-cells almost as broad as long; egg-shell bearing long spines mostly divided at tips → vulgaris. B. Tentacles much longer than column even at rest; basal part constricted; largest nettle-cells considerably longer than broad; egg-shell smooth or bearing short simple spines → oligactis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply colour (presence/absence of chlorophyll bodies), tentacle length relative to column, nettle-cell proportions, and egg-shell ornamentation in combination to identify species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus Hydra diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Freshwater polyps which produce eggs with hard chitinous shells; habitually anchored by the aboral disk but possess considerable powers of locomotion; extremely contractile and variable in form and size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of chitinous-shelled eggs and combination of anchorage plus locomotion and contractility to delimit genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family Hydridæ characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Small Eleutheroblastea in which the mouth is surrounded by hollow tentacles. Permanent colonies are not formed, but reproduction by budding commonly takes place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family-level identification rests on solitary polyp habit, hollow tentacles around mouth, and frequent budding; absence of permanent colonies distinguishes Hydridæ from colonial hydrozoans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nettle-cell (nematocyst) morphology and seasonal variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Capsules with barbed threads are variable in size but usually broad in proportion to length and nearly spherical; barbed threads are long and slender with a basal circle of stout spines (usually 4) and smaller obscure spines above; capsules with unbarbed threads are broadly oval. Measured largest capsules: winter ~0.0189 mm breadth × 0.019 mm length; summer smaller (~0.012 mm breadth). Malformed corpuscles are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nematocyst morphology (shape, presence/absence of barbs, spine arrangement, measurements) is a key diagnostic and seasonal character—compare measurements and morphology between specimens and seasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproductive organs and sexual dimorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproductive organs confined to upper part of body. In Indian specimens sexes are distinct; spermaries are produced more readily than ovaries; ovaries and spermaries not found on same individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual state can be used diagnostically; sampling time and conditions (e.g., approach of hot weather) affect presence of spermaries/ovaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal broods and morphological differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Two broods in Calcutta: cold-weather brood (larger, stouter, more deeply coloured, buds more freely, larger nematocysts, usually 6 tentacles) and hot-weather brood (smaller, slender, paler, buds sparingly, smaller nematocysts, usually 4–5 tentacles). Only cold-weather form known to become sexually mature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish seasonal forms by size, colour, tentacle number, nematocyst size, and reproductive activity; beware of confusing tropical steady-state forms with seasonal phases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budding pattern and positional order
rubrics_metrics.description: Buds are confined to a narrow zone nearer the base than the apex. Each quadrant of the column can produce a single bud in a definite zone; buds of different quadrants are not produced simultaneously. If quadrants are north, east, south, west and the first bud is north, second will be east, third south, fourth west. Usually not more than two buds present simultaneously; about three weeks elapse from bud appearance to liberation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bud position, quadrant order and timing (≈3 weeks to liberation) as characters in life-history observations and when comparing populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of reproduction: budding, fission, sexual
rubrics_metrics.description: Budding is the usual form of reproduction; sexual reproduction (eggs) occurs but is less common in India. Reproduction by fission occurs rarely—equal vertical fission involves circumoral area lengthening, extra tentacles, constriction of mouth and vertical division; unequal vertical fission rare; transverse fission not observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record reproductive mode frequencies; note morphological sequence during fission (tentacle increase, mouth constriction) to confirm fission events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locomotion and attachment mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Polyp can float free or attach by basal disk. Crawling: polyp bends column, extends tentacles, attaches tentacle tips by adhesive secretion, liberates basal disk and drags column forward; tentacles can be used to pull across gaps by fixing tip, freeing basal disk, contracting tentacle. Attachment also effected by gland-cell secretions on tentacle tips. Floating individuals may be attached to minute objects by basal disk or mucus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe tentacle adhesion, basal-disk behaviour, and sequence of attachment-release when documenting movement; adhesive gland-cell secretion is important for substrate fixation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeding behaviour and digestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Tentacles capture prey (chiefly chironomid and may-fly larvae, small copepod and phyllopod crustacea). Captured prey is paralysed by nematocysts, brought to mouth, enveloped in mucus extruded from digestive cavity; gland-cells pour digestive fluid on bulky food; soluble products fall to bottom of cavity and digested by endoderm cells; insoluble parts are ejected without reaching base of cavity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prey spectrum, mucus extrusion, and two-stage digestion (extracavity fluid digestion + endoderm cell digestion) as behavioral and physiological diagnostic observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouration linked to digestion and reproductive state
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour appears mainly due to digestive products. Brown/orange individuals take 3–4 days to digest food; in aquaria colour is lost and digestion is more rapid. Starved individuals are nearly colourless. Egg-producing individuals often dark green and retain colour in captivity; sperm-producing individuals often lose colour and may become milky due to liquid droplets in endoderm cells.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret coloration carefully: it reflects feeding state and reproductive condition rather than fixed pigmentation; use colour as an indirect indicator of recent feeding or reproductive status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habitat preference and geographical distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: H. vulgaris in India usually found in stagnant water with aquatic vegetation (e.g., Limnanthemum, Lemna); also recorded from pools of rain-water on seashore near Madras. Distribution given for many Indian localities; genus occurs only in fresh or brackish water and is universally distributed (viridis absent in Oriental region in records).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use habitat (stagnant, vegetated ponds) and local records when surveying; expect microhabitat shifts with temperature (surface vs deeper shady parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medusoid generation presence/absence as life-cycle trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hydroids lack a free medusoid generation (e.g., Cordylophora lacustris, medusoid suppressed in Bimeria vestita; Cordylophora does not produce free medusæ). Others possess both hydroid and medusoid generations (e.g., Microhydra ryderi reproduces by direct budding and gives rise to medusæ that become sexually mature). In several genera only the medusa is known and the hydroid generation is doubtful or unknown (e.g., Limnocodium sowerbii, Limnocodium kawaii, Limnocnida tanganyikæ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record presence/absence of medusoid stage as a key taxonomic and life-history character; absence may be genuine or due to incomplete knowledge—note whether medusae or hydroid stage were observed and in what environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polypodium hydriforme multi-stage life-history
rubrics_metrics.description: Two stages known: (a) a spiral ribbon-like form parasitic on sterlet (Acipenser ruthenus) eggs; (b) a small Hydra-like form with both filamentous and club-shaped tentacles. Life-history incomplete (additional stage later described by Lippen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When encountering unusual forms associated with fish eggs, consider Polypodium-like parasitism; document multiple morphological stages to resolve life history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glossary/technical term definitions for morphological description
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions provided for key terms used in descriptions: Aboral (basal) disk; Cnidoblast (living cell of nematocyst); Cnidocil (minute bristle associated with nettle-cell); Column (upright part of polyp); Ectoderm (external cell-layer); Endoderm (internal cell-layer); Green (chlorophyll) corpuscles; Mesogloea (gelatinous intermediate layer); Nettle-cell (nematocyst) (cell capsule containing an eversible thread); Oral disk/Peristome (eminence surrounding mouth); Polyp (individual coelenterate fixed by one end with mouth at other); Tentacles (filamentous outgrowths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these standardized definitions when recording morphological characters to ensure consistent descriptions and comparability across specimens and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic description of Hydra vulgaris (phase orientalis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colour variable (pale in summer, deep orange/dull brown/dark green in winter); cells lack spherical/oval coloured bodies. Column slender, elongate, often cylindrical, sometimes wine-glass shaped when with food. Tentacles usually 4–6 (occasionally 8), slender when extended; at rest not much longer than body but capable of very great extension. Nettle-cells thickly set on surface giving hirsute appearance. Reproductive organs confined to upper body; eggs with long spines on shell; buds usually 4–5 tentacles at liberation; cold-weather vs hot-weather brood differences described. Indian specimens differ from European ones: sexes invariably distinct; nematocysts invariably smaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the combination of colour variation, tentacle number and behavior, nettle-cell arrangement and size, reproductive organ presence, and brood/seasonal characteristics to diagnose H. vulgaris and its tropical phase (orientalis).
